cards.front: Recall a key point about Lighting and Flash
cards.back: Light direction dramatically changes a subject: front light = flat, even; side light = texture and depth; back light = rim lighting or silhouette.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Lighting and Flash
cards.back: Light quality: hard light (direct sun, bare flash) creates sharp shadows; soft light (overcast, softbox) creates gentle gradients.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Lighting and Flash
cards.back: The golden hour (just after sunrise/before sunset) produces warm, directional, soft light — ideal for many subjects.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Lighting and Flash
cards.back: Flash can fill shadows, freeze motion or be the primary light source — but on-camera flash creates flat, unflattering light.

cards.front: What should you know about photography exam tips?
cards.back: Show the LIGHT SETUP for each photograph — include diagrams if possible. Annotate with LIGHTING vocabulary (key light, fill, rim, hard, soft). Explain the MOOD created by each lighting approach. Compare natural and artificial light results.

Students often make mistakes with this topic. Wrong: You need expensive studio lights to take good photographs. Correct: Natural light is often the BEST light source — window light, golden hour and open shade all produce beautiful, professional-quality results without any equipment. Understanding light DIRECTION and QUALITY is far more important than owning expensive lighting gear.

Photograph the same subject using at least three different lighting setups (e.g. natural side light, backlit silhouette, diffused window light). Annotate each describing the light quality, direction and mood created.

cards.front: Assessment Objective Focus: Lighting and Flash
cards.back: AO1 — Knowledge: Demonstrate knowledge of Lighting and Flash using appropriate art vocabulary. Identify techniques, materials and processes accurately.

cards.front: Understanding Lighting and Flash in Context
cards.back: Lighting and Flash is a fundamental aspect of GCSE Art and Design that connects to all four AQA assessment objectives. Understanding this topic requires both practical skill and contextual knowledge — you must apply techniques effectively AND explain how your work relates to other artists and designers. The AQA specification requires you to develop ideas (AO1), refine work through experimentation

For lighting and flash, effective experimentation means testing multiple approaches systematically. Start by researching how professional artists approach lighting and flash, replicate their techniques as studies, then adapt and combine approaches to develop your own method. The AQA mark scheme rewards purposeful experimentation — random undocumented attempts score lower than systematic investigat

The AQA assessment objective AO4 requires a ‘personal, meaningful response’ — your work should express your own ideas and viewpoints, not simply replicate what you have seen. Identify what specifically interests you about lighting and flash, consider what you want to communicate, make creative choices that reflect your intention, and evaluate whether your outcome successfully expresses your ideas.
